title: 2 Kings 18:13–25
context: In Hezekiah’s fourteenth year Sennacherib of Assyria takes the fortified cities of Judah, and Hezekiah first pays a heavy tribute, stripping silver from the LORD’s house and gold from the temple doors. Assyria nonetheless sends the Tartan, the Rabsaris, and the Rabshakeh, commonly understood as official titles, with an army to Jerusalem, where the Rabshakeh mocks Judah’s confidence in Egypt, twists Hezekiah’s removal of the high places into an offense against the LORD, and claims that the LORD sent him. The same events are told in Isaiah 36–37 and summarized in 2 Chronicles 32, each with its own emphasis; the existing boxes at Isaiah 36–37 treat that parallel. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly treat the taunts as shared ground about where true trust belongs (compare Psalm 20:7; Isaiah 31:1). Neither tradition generally builds a contrast on the political choices here; both read the chapter as a test of faith in the LORD.

verses.text: Now in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and took them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Sennacherib taking all the fortified cities of Judah in Hezekiah’s fourteenth year. Even a faithful king faces severe trials.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the invasion as a test permitted by God for his own purposes (compare Isaiah 10:5). Readers in both traditions commonly hold the date with caution, given the difficult chronology.

verses.text: Hezekiah king of Judah sent to the king of Assyria at Lachish, saying, “I have offended you. Withdraw from me. That which you put on me, I will bear.” The king of Assyria appointed to Hezekiah king of Judah three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah admitting he has offended and agreeing to pay a heavy tribute. Fear and pressure lead him to seek peace by payment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his submission as a moment of weakness before he turns fully to the LORD. Both traditions commonly read the tribute as a very large payment, without pressing exact modern equivalents.

verses.text: Hezekiah gave him all the silver that was found in the LORD’s house and in the treasures of the king’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah giving silver from the LORD’s house and the royal treasury. The cost of appeasement is high.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the stripping of the temple as a painful sign of the crisis. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse without passing a final verdict on Hezekiah’s decision.

verses.text: At that time, Hezekiah cut off the gold from the doors of the LORD’s temple, and from the pillars which Hezekiah king of Judah had overlaid, and gave it to the king of Assyria.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah cutting the gold from the temple doors he had overlaid himself. The reformer gives away what he once adorned.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the irony as underlining how deeply the crisis pressed on Judah. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that tribute did not secure lasting peace.

verses.text: The king of Assyria sent Tartan, Rabsaris, and Rabshakeh from Lachish to King Hezekiah with a great army to Jerusalem. They went up and came to Jerusalem. When they had come up, they came and stood by the conduit of the upper pool, which is in the highway of the fuller’s field.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Assyrian officials arriving with a great army and standing by the conduit of the upper pool. The threat comes to the city itself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the location as a pointed setting, recalling Isaiah’s earlier encounter with Ahaz (Isaiah 7:3). Readers in both traditions commonly hold the exact site with caution.

verses.text: When they had called to the king, Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebnah the scribe, and Joah the son of Asaph the recorder came out to them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Eliakim, Shebnah, and Joah going out to meet the Assyrians. Royal officials represent the king in a dangerous negotiation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the delegation as Hezekiah’s careful response to the threat. Both traditions commonly read the verse as setting up the speech that follows.

verses.text: Rabshakeh said to them, “Say now to Hezekiah, ‘The great king, the king of Assyria, says, “What confidence is this in which you trust?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Rabshakeh asking what confidence Hezekiah trusts in. The question goes to the heart of the matter: where does Judah’s trust lie?
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the question as unintentionally raising the central theme of the chapter. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a challenge to faith.

verses.text: You say (but they are but vain words), ‘There is counsel and strength for war.’ Now on whom do you trust, that you have rebelled against me?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Rabshakeh dismissing Judah’s talk of counsel and strength as vain words. He mocks human planning and power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his mockery as exposing how fragile human strength is apart from God. Both traditions commonly read the verse as preparing to show where real strength lies.

verses.text: Now, behold, you trust in the staff of this bruised reed, even in Egypt. If a man leans on it, it will go into his hand and pierce it. So is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust on him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Rabshakeh calling Egypt a bruised reed that pierces the hand of anyone who leans on it. Even an enemy can speak a true word about false trust.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image echoing prophetic warnings against relying on Egypt (compare Isaiah 31:1). Readers in both traditions commonly apply the verse to any trust placed in human power.

verses.text: But if you tell me, ‘We trust in the LORD our God,’ isn’t that he whose high places and whose altars Hezekiah has taken away, and has said to Judah and to Jerusalem, ‘You shall worship before this altar in Jerusalem’?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Rabshakeh twisting Hezekiah’s removal of the high places into an offense against the LORD. Truth is distorted to undermine faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the taunt as misunderstanding worship at the place the LORD chose (compare Deuteronomy 12:5). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a deliberate attempt to confuse the people.

verses.text: Now therefore, please give pledges to my master the king of Assyria, and I will give you two thousand horses if you are able on your part to set riders on them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Rabshakeh offering two thousand horses if Judah can find riders for them. He mocks Judah’s weakness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the taunt as emphasizing Judah’s helplessness apart from the LORD (compare Psalm 20:7). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as calculated humiliation.

verses.text: How then can you turn away the face of one captain of the least of my master’s servants, and put your trust on Egypt for chariots and for horsemen?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Rabshakeh asking how Judah could resist even the least Assyrian captain while trusting Egypt. Human resources look hopeless.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as stripping away every false support. Both traditions commonly read it as setting the stage for trust in the LORD alone.

verses.text: Have I now come up without the LORD against this place to destroy it? The LORD said to me, ‘Go up against this land, and destroy it.’ ” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Rabshakeh claiming that the LORD sent him to destroy the land. He uses God’s name to weaken resistance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD did use Assyria as an instrument (Isaiah 10:5), yet the Rabshakeh’s claim serves his own propaganda. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a half-truth that the following chapters correct (compare Isaiah 10:12).
